paragraphs.heading: Sediment into rock
paragraphs.text: Lithification is the transformation of poorly consolidated sediments into sedimentary rock. It belongs to a wider process called diagenesis: the physical and chemical changes that sediments go through after they are deposited. The first causes of those changes are compaction, microbial activity and interactions between water and rock.

paragraphs.heading: Squeezing and cementing
paragraphs.text: After deposition, sediments are compacted as layer after layer of new sediment buries them. They are also cemented by minerals that precipitate from solution. In the early stages, lithification comes with a drop in porosity and, in clay sediments, the expulsion of water, while the main mineral assemblages stay unaltered. Porosity usually goes down during diagenesis, except in rare cases such as when minerals dissolve.

paragraphs.heading: Where it starts and stops
paragraphs.text: Diagenesis does not include weathering, which is alteration at the surface, or deep metamorphism. There is no sharp line between diagenesis and metamorphism, but metamorphism happens at higher temperatures and pressures. Raised pressure and temperature only begin to matter once sediments are buried much deeper in the Earth's crust.

paragraphs.heading: Swapped minerals
paragraphs.text: During diagenesis, other minerals can take the place of sediment grains, rock fragments and fossils. Calcite, siderite and pyrite are examples. Many things influence the outcome. They include hydrothermal solutions, groundwater, the porosity and permeability of the rock, dissolution and precipitation reactions, and time.

paragraphs.heading: What happens to buried life
paragraphs.text: When animal or plant matter is buried during sedimentation, its organic molecules break down as temperature and pressure rise. This takes place in the first few hundred meters of burial and yields two main products, kerogens and bitumens. It is generally accepted that hydrocarbons form when heat alters these kerogens.

paragraphs.heading: Why geologists study it
paragraphs.text: Studying diagenesis in rocks helps show the geologic history they have been through. It also shows the nature and type of the fluids that have moved through them. On the commercial side, such studies help judge how likely it is that economically viable mineral and hydrocarbon deposits will be found.
